newsitem.title: TAIWAN: HK handover could help Taiwan-China impasse-report.
newsitem.headline: HK handover could help Taiwan-China impasse-report.

text.p: Taiwan's media on Friday was abuzz with speculation that the ceremony marking Hong Kong's return to China would create an opportunity for Taipei and Beijing to break a bitter 24-month political impasse.
Several local media outlets reported that top negotiators from Taipei and Beijing could hold an informal meeting in Hong Kong before attending a handover gala at midnight on June 30.

Such a meeting would be the first in four years between Koo Chen-fu, chairman of Taiwan's Straits Exchange Foundation, and his counterpart Wang Daohan of Beijing's Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Strait.

The two men held historic talks in Singapore on April 29, 1993, the first public Taiwan-China meeting since a 1949 civil war that left the mainland in communist control and Chinese Nationalists fleeing to Taiwan.
The Singapore meeting heralded a flurry of semi-official gatherings on a range of civilian issues from 1993 to 1995.

Koo and Wang had arranged to meet again in June 1995, but the plan collapsed after Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui paid a private but high-profile visit to the United States -- angering Beijing so much that it suspended the talks.
China, which has viewed Taiwan as a renegade province, said Lee's U.S. visit was an attempt to promote independence for Taiwan rather than reunification with the mainland.
The informal Taiwan-China dialogue remains on ice.
Asked about the possibility of a Hong Kong ice-breaker, the Taipei foundation declined to comment, saying Koo had not even received an invitation to the handover ceremony.
In Beijing, an official at Wang's office said Wang did not rule out the possibility that he and Koo may meet, but added Wang had not decided whether to witness the handover ceremony.
"If they both go, it's natural for the two old friends to greet each other," the official told Taiwan state television by telephone in Beijing.
Taiwan said on Wednesday it would not let officials witness the handover ceremony if attendance came at the expense of the island's diplomatic dignity.
Kao Koong-lian, vice chairman of the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council, said whoever Hong Kong or Beijing invites to represent Taiwan could accept only if accorded proper respect.
Kao made clear this meant treating Nationalist-ruled Taiwan as something other than a mere province of the communist People's Republic of China.
Taipei maintains that its Chinese Nationalist republic has status equal to that of China's national government.
Taiwan has repeatedly urged China to resume talks to resolve thorny issues facing both sides, including fishing disputes and repatriation of hijackers and stowaways.
Beijing has consistently declined, saying no talks were possible until Taiwan showed its sincerity by dropping what it regards as Taipei's "splittist" activities.
